Messages.Author: Wes
Messages.Body:
I was giving some thought to the whole anti-weenie discussion and came up
with this general use master card. Let me know what you think.

==============================
The Hunger

Master Out-of-Turn

You may play this card during your turn. Place this card on a vampire that
has a capacity above 7 and has less than 3 blood on her. The vampire with
this card taps and enters combat with a vampire controlled by another
methuselah with a capacity below 4. The vampire with this card has +2
strength for the duration of this combat. Any blood lost by the opposing
vampire goes to the vampire with this card at the end of each round. If the
opposing vampire is not ready at the end of this combat, this vampire
untaps. Burn this card at the end of combat.

===============================

Thematically, this card represents the hunger that ancient vampires have for
the blood of younger vampires. After centuries of unlife, the blood of
normal humans no longer sates them and they start to crave the vitae of
their younger brethren. This is also why many vampires fear the
antedilluveans.

The rationale behind this card is that you can basically force someone
else's vampire to fight a weenie for you.

That vampire can potentially gain from this situation so it is not
necessarily bad to have it played against you.

It is meant to be a weenie-killer obviously, and since the effect occurs
outside of the normal turn structure, it could conceivably slow down a
weenie deck without adversely affecting the non-weenie Methuselahs.

It could also be used in more of a co-operative way than a coercive way,
which is an aspect of the game that I believe could be expanded on somewhat.

Additionally, because the vampire this card is played on must have less than
3 blood, it could be used offensively against someone who has just Minion
Tapped.

Example.

LARRY --> Minion Tap Arika down to 1
WES --> Cool. I play The Hunger to force Arika to fight Gillian Krader
LARRY --> Damn you to hell.

Play in conjunction with Frenzy and Save Face for Fun +2!

Thoughts?

(As usual, this card is public domain and White Wolf is welcome to have it
or whatever... I give up the rights to it. Does this even help or am I
talking out of my ass again?)

Cheers,
WES

well. You need two MPAs... granted, not hard but now there is less focus to

right type of opponents. I don't see this card becoming the core of any

> Torpor it. Force it to rush Watenda via The Hunger. Disguised weapon.

afraid of Disguised Weapon, Ivory Bow, Amaranth myself. Call a blood hunt on

card-intensive and not likely to work all that often.

The more I think about it though, the more it seems like something that
should be playable only on your own guys. Consider this... without Anson or
Parthenon etc you could not simply Minion Tap/Hunger somebody. Possibly
workable?

What about this? During the combat, no combat cards can be played. This
gives less protection to the weenie but in turn means the elder vampire is
less likely to get destroyed themselves. The idea is to whack-a-mole the
weenies and give the older vampire a slight edge. More or less.

Thanks for the input!

Cheers,

Messages.Author: James Coupe

In message <3c8d771a...@netnews.attbi.com>,

berni...@attbi.comHOLDLeSPAM writes:

And whilst you can provide many things it can do well, you have failed
to note that it can't do everything that any other discipline can do -
something of which you are well aware, most certainly.

As a result, I am at a loss as to why you are lying about this, unless
you are attempting hyperbole badly.

Going through your categories:

Bleed: It cannot, for instance, combine bleed with pool gain. Other
disciplines have the ability to bleed other Methuselahs
(Obfuscate, Dementation)

Politics: You masterfully provide a number of things Dominate can do,
and then spectacularly fail to note that Kindred Co-ercion and
Pulling Strings are reactions. It is also notable that Ventrue
Antitribu are not Dominate. :( You cannot outmatch Presence or
Melpominee on forward facing votes. You effectively cannot use
Dominate to pass your own votes. You cannot use Dominate to
gain pool when your own votes pass (Presence). You cannot use
Dominate to cancel the votes of others when calling votes
(Auspex).

Contesting: Certainly, this is one of Dominate's slowly facilitated
strengths. (That is, it wasn't originally.) It is notable
that, if you can invoke Ventrue Antitribu above, then the
Lasombra can do similar things here with locations. There is
also Betrayer (as you note, which still isn't Dominate) and
Blood Siege for non-identical, but analogous, situations.

Combat: Dominate can avoid combat quite well, under the right
circumstances. (That is, a deck can plan for it, but it won't
just happen.) It can Dodge, but the fall-back level of Absorb
the Mind isn't that brilliant (though, certainly, a good example
of how fallback levels should work). If you're playing
Dominate, you probably wouldn't include Absorb the Mind, though
you would if you were playing myt/dom, which is slightly
different. Thoughts Betrayed is good, if expensive

Now, of course, Dominate also has Imaginary Card one which will
deal aggravated damage (Protean, Potence, Vicissitude). It also
has Made Up Card which will prevent damage. It, further, has
I'm Ignoring What Cards Exist which is excellent for ending
combat once you're in there (because you weren't untapped or
woken). It can also use that much maligned card, We're Making
It Up As We Go Along, for considerable maneuvering power and
This Card Wasn't Even Designed Let Alone Printed provides an
excellent source of additional strikes.

Combat is *obviously* one arena where Dominate can, in your
words, "[do] everything that any other discipline can do".
Quite clearly so.

Bounce: Telepathic Misdirection and My Enemy's Enemy exist, but in
general Redirection and Deflection are, indeed, the better
choice. Of course, if we're looking more generally at bleed
*defence*, then Dominate is far from the only option. Folderol,
Telepathic Counter, Folderol, various Chimerstry cards and
Folderol all provide useful bleed reduction.

Stealing: Locations and vampires, yes. Of course, you need to have the
vampires in torpor for Graverobbing, which is not an
inconsiderable effort. Corruption, Form of Corruption and
Temptation provide a very different strategy for the Setites.
Combat defence will save you from Graverobbing but it cannot
save you from the Setites. Mind Rape has the delay, and
requires older vampires, which is also to be considered.

Need Pool: With specified actions, yes, you can gain pool. What you
can't do is gain pool as a by-product of other actions, which
Necromancy (Tower of London) and Presence (Social Charm et al)
can do well, and a couple of other deck styles can have a go at
with Bribes, Anathema and so on (though votes will make Presence
useful, though not essential).

Tap Minions: Sure, though a number of other disciplines also have this
option down quite nicely.

Stealth: Certain amounts of bleed based stealth, sure. And certain
amounts of "you can't block" is excellent, but not the same.

Now, let's go round a few other things:

Intercept: One of the fundamentals of the game, and something that
Dominate just can't do. Sure, you can pair it off with
something else but your assertion that Dominate can do
"everything that any other discipline can do" and, when
challenged, "it IS true" don't add up to pairing things off with
other disciplines. Dominate cannot help with any intercept.

Real stealth: You want arbitrary stealth for other actions. Not every
deck is playing simple bleeds, so Bonding and Kine Dominance are
not the best of options. (For instance, the pool gain actions
you cite cannot benefit from them.)

Card recycling: Necromancy par excellence, of course, but also available
to political action focused decks, which Dominate cannot let you
pass, only react to.

Untap: Thaumaturgy, Fortitude, Temporis, Presence and so on are not
Dominate, as much as you might like them to be. Whether you can
combine with them or not is not relevant to Dominate's ability
to do "everything that any other discipline can do". Dominate
cannot provide you with arbitrary amounts of untap, via
permanent additional actions, transient untaps (either
defensive, or active) or so on.

Millstone: A number of millstone options are available to different
disciplines - for instance, Auspex's minor fun in Revelations,
through Raptor and Feline Saboteur.

Reconnaissance: Auspex is good here - what's in their hand, combined
with discard from Revelations - though Owl Companion certainly
has its uses.

Blood gain: Necromancy and Fortitude work well here. They're certainly
reasons why you might play things that aren't dominate, per your
original assertion. Restoration, Regeneration, Rapid Healing,
Summon Soul etc.

Blood loss: Thaumaturgy and Obtenebration, along with active indepedent
vote decks for Free States Rant, have excellent options
available for blood loss, combined with Society of Leopold,
Daemonic Possession and so on. Obviously, this is something
that Dominate "can do, and often better".

and so on. Just go round disciplines and find interesting, fairly
unique things they can do.

So, when you said that Dominate can "do everything that any other
discipline can do", re-asserting this with "it IS true", I can only
assume you were ignoring the facts of what the cards do for some unknown
reason. :(

Your brain appears to be equating combat avoidance with damage

Seduction is, of course, limited to one per action. Thus you will find
yourself with fewer options regarding other blocking vampires, if you're
relying on Seduction and Obedience.

Obedience requires an older vampire for use, and this limits its ability
when non-weenified combat enters an arena. (For instance, Eurobrujah
Vote/Combat decks, Tzimisce decks, Gangrel royalty decks and so on, all
of which have shown themselves repeatedly as viable archetypes.)

Gargoyles will also provide you with some, erm, interesting problems, at
least, with intelligent play.

DoC makes it much harder for you to do anything substantial to them in
response, though their ability to advance in combat requires careful
consideration.

It can cancel certain impending combats, and if you believe that
Thoughts Betrayed is serious combat *defence* then you're just ignoring
the facts of what other decks can do.

When you are in combat, you lose two blood to Thoughts Betrayed, which
you are unlikely to gain back. (Bearing in mind, of course, that this
use requires DOM, which is different from the weenie dom/DOM situation
that was notioned a few posts back.) This is, in itself, not
inconsiderable.

The Brujah can, of course, throw down Torn Signpost and Blur. Thoughts
Betrayed does nothing. The Tzimisce have similarly styled options.
Weapon decks have weapons, and additional strikes, and will be mildly
hampered by not being able to play, say, Undead Strength, but you've
just paid two blood anyway, which might as well be two damage for all
the difference it will make. Toreador-esque gun decks (most likely as a
sideline to another option, given the difficulties, though Telepathic
Tracking is a potentially potent option) do well here, similarly the
!Tor hand damage decks that have been gone over again recently, playing
the Art of Pain and so on. The Gangrel do lose the really quite nice
option of Scorpion Sting (a pity) but do have the not inconsiderable
asset of Carrion Crows and claws, sufficient to torporise someone
arrogant enough to believe that Thoughts Betrayed was sufficient defence
for when people catch you.

The Assamites are different, in that most of their power *does* come
from strikes. Certainly, Thoughts Betrayed is a potent defence against
this. (And it certainly seems it was intentional to develop this side
in Final Nights, from where I stand.)

Taking situations where Obedience is useful - weeniefied rush - you need
to be playing slightly older vampires. This makes weenie dom/DOM less
viable in this instance. However, assuming you're tapped, they rush
you, enter combat, you die. So you need to untap or wake *or* already
be untapped. (As covered elsewhere, Dominate has no useful sources of
untap in this manner, though Obedience will "not tap" you if you were
untapped.) This means another resource down - either an action
potentially missed, or a Wake used for defence in that option that could
otherwise have been used for, say, Deflection - an important trade-off,
given that you lack serious bleed defence in other ways, being unable to
take out other serious bleeders, for instance.

But in any event, weenified rush can result in situations where you're
facing three or four rushes a turn, with careful use of Haven
Uncovereds. (Where an intelligent player picks a vampire who is tapped,
so your untapped would-be Obedience fodder can't come in, because they
can't block the +1 stealth.)

This is untrue. :(

Had I wanted to focus on combat, I would have done so. Combat was one
topic among lots. However, because combat has so many diverse options
it is certainly easier to make the point that you're basic assertion is
fundamentally flawed.

>I'll say it up front, Dominate
>(on it's own) will not be able to hit harder than a combat oriented
>deck. Point is that they don't need to.

No, they don't need to.

That's not the point you initially made, however, which was that
Dominate could do everything other disciplines could do, and sometimes
better. Certainly, Presence doesn't need to be able to deal out
aggravated damage, but then no-one was claiming that Presence could do
everything Protean (or whatever) could do.

You're seemingly attempting to prejudge other people's options.
Dominate certainly has its place in multiple useful deck-styles (either
heavily focused, or not). It is not, however, the only deck style or,
indeed, the only viable deck-style. Lasombra's deck archive is a
testament to that.

Someone whose metagame is substantially shifted in such a fashion as you
need to be able to hit out combatively (or defend with 100% accuracy) or
DIE (these things happen) will find many reasons to avoid Dominate as an
all-curing panacea.

Someone whose ability with combat is such that they find themselves much
more able to control a table sufficiently for a table-win (for instance,
they can quickly despatch a prey, followed by waiting until they're down
to the final two and just kill the other player for 3VPs for a table
win, able to manipulate and distract people in the mean-time ("Oh, it
was just a lucky flow of cards. It's a bit combo intensive, I mean,
look, I'm having to discard <X>, <Y> and <Z>")) will find many reasons
to avoid Dominate because Dominate is not a generally useful discipline
for advancing in combat. (Of course, certain corner cases exist, where
players have skilfully used the inferior version of Thoughts Betrayed to
great effect when the cards have turned up right.)

Those wanting to control their position on the table - in terms of
physicality - will need to move forward into Presence and may, as a
result, shift away from Dominate. Calling votes is not something to
which Dominate is well-suited. Few would note political decks as being
non-viable in most non-metagame specific circumstances - it is certainly
possible to play political decks well.

It is certainly a poor player who has not considered what happens when a
rush is foiled. (As can happen with many decks.) Inclusion of hand-
cycling mechanisms and careful use of discard phases, along with
repeated drawing out of your defence in less intensive manners (with,
for instance, Haven Uncovered) is not exactly uncommon for any people
with a handle on the situation.

Offensive, *productive* combat is a difficult style to play. History
shows us that it is certainly possible, however.

Riffing is a musical term. It means, loosely, variations of a set. I'd
thought this would be obvious in the context, but I'm glad to clarify it
for you, since you asked. Now, to the actual substance....

Anarch Revolts: you've probably never heard the term "Riding the
wave," either. Anarch revolt: everybody lose 1. Weenies: I'm spending a
hell of a lot less pool for my vampires than anyone else but another
weenie-player. Ride the wave home. It's a little trickier than that, but
it does work. Not %100, but nothing is.

Politics: you are going to Majesty out when you get blocked, anyway. If
you've got some light blood gain, like HG, or (more likely) Blood Doll,
then you have the option of being untapped and ready to act again. The
votes are just spice with some BO if you need it, but you can likely sell
the vote on the spare point that's going to go.... somewhere. Probably
not as good as just doing straight bleed, but I've seen it do well.

As to "seeing this do well," just crawl out from under that rock and take
a look at Lasombra's tournament winning deck archive. FoS are not
especially small-cap, and they aren't even in the same league as
weenie-presence bleed (i.e. they ain't broken).

Vote defence can be attempted using Kindred Co-ercion, Pulling Strings
and so on. This is not perfect, however. Delaying Tactics often proves
to be better defence. In low powered vote environments, you can't, for
instance, affect the votes of Ventrue Headquarters or political action
cards.

Combat defence can be attempted with Obedience. This requires the
vampire being rushed to be untapped, or woken, and to be older. These
can all be attempted, but none is a given. Thoughts Betrayed provides
certain elements of combat defence. Absorb the Mind can be useful, but
Dodge! may be better unless all your vampires will definitely have
Dominate. (For instance, you may later want to repeat a Mind Rape to do
something else with the stolen vampire, and their being torporised might
not be of use to you. Or you may be playing a primarily Dominate based
deck, but with one or two less obvious situations occurring - though in
a mono-Dominate deck, it is usable.)

Seduction is a different kettle of fish - attempting to prevent you from
being blocked. This is difficult if any undirected actions are to be
attempted, though a Dominate deck may be doing substantial numbers of
directed actions, of course. Eagle's Sight, and so forth, may come into
play, though this is not a given in any environment but they can throw
sufficient curve-balls from any deck which is doing minor intercepting
(for instance, random Tzimisce decks, doing Pulse/Changeling, along with
some intercept and combat and taste.)

Dominate has habitually been one of the stronger disciplines played
mono. Fortitude also has its place. (I recall a thread on this some
time ago. The combat defence, blood gain, bleed and unblockability that
Fortitude garnered was considered especially important, dealing with a
range of things in a very different way.)

Doing a google search for "Crypt Machine" should provide a decklist,
at some point. It might even be on one of the deck archive sites.

At heart, though, it's:

All of the vampires of capacity 3 or less with dominate, Isabel
Giovanni, and Ingrid Russo (the two 4-capacity vampires with DOM).

* A few dominate skill cards
* assorted other masters to taste, probably including either Info
Highway, Effective Management, and Sudden Reversal
* Lots of Govern the Unaligned
* Threats (? That's what I'd include, anyway, as opposed to
Conditioning, though Foreshadowing Destruction would also be good)
* maybe Bonding or Seduction/The Sleeping Mind
* maybe some wake/Deflection
* maybe a little light combat defense (disciplineless dodge/maneuver),
but this can be left alone
* maybe some Delaying Tactics

It can pretty much be built with all common/uncommon cards. General
strategy involves bringing up one of the vampires with DOM, or getting
out a 3-capacity vampire and slapping a skill card on that one, then
getting more vampires out for free. Eventually, just swarm bleed
everyone to death.

It is definitely a strong deck, but it mostly relies on speed and lots
and lots of actions to win, rather than any inherent skill at
surviving other deck styles.

> Currently I'm not quite digging how it deals with combat and vote decks.

It doesn't deal with the former, except through multiple expendable
minions. Combat kills it, but often not fast enough. It could splash
some Obedience in, as a capacity of 4 is larger than some weenie
decks, but this will generally not be useful.

With the latter, it can use Delaying Tactics to stave off any really
nasty votes, and hopefully survive to the next turn, in which it might
gain more pool (with superior Govern) or in which it might oust its
prey.

cf. Google search for "Crypt Machine", deck listing thereof.

The variants you will find range from the original version many years
ago (disciplineless Dodge as combat defense, Pulling Strings as vote
defense) to the ultra-fast version played by Patrick O'Shea at the
Atlanta qualifier (60 cards, no vote defense, no combat defense, bleeds
for ~15 per turn) to variants utilizing Gloria Giovanni and
miscellaneous others. All share the same basic characteristics:

1) use of small-capacity Dominate vampires
2) use of superior Govern the Unaligned to avoid paying very much, and
in some cases anything at all for additional vampires past #1
3) heavy use of ALL Dominate bleed cards and modifiers
4) heavy use of Seduction and Sleeping Mind to avoid being caught
5) heavy use of Deflection, since almost every deck will eventually
bleed you

The "classic" version makes use of 12 four-cap vampires with inferior
Dominate, and a bunch of skill cards in the deck. The first one out
gets a skill card on turn 2, and plays superior Govern on the second.
One transfer is made to each of 3 remaining vamps, the second vamp comes
out. Turn 3, the second vamp gets a skill card, both play superior
Govern (with Seduction if necessary) -- 2 more vamps come out, spend 4
transfers and 1 pool to see the 5th.

At the start of turn 4, you have spent 8 pool (including the 1 pool to
see a crypt vamp), and have 4 vampires with Dominate. Some decks will
have just gotten their first or second vampire. Normally at this point
the deck empties its hand of any card with chain-links on it, bleeding
for a ridiculous amount. Wakes, Deflections, etc. will slow down the
relatively inevitable, and intercept wall decks that are using their
head CAN kill it, as long as they have a way around Seduction. Its
defense against most things is simply "have more pool and more minions
than they can easily get rid of".

Ways to stop it? Have early +1 intercept available to more than one
vampire and stop the superior Govern actions. Be able to Deflect lots.
Be able to pool-gain lots. Be able to Rush vampires lots. Toolbox
decks generally just get run over. Many focused decks also get run
over, because the definition of "lots" really is "lots".

Playing this thing is tantamount to putting a large bullseye on your
forehead, taping a $20 to it, and daring the table to come get you. In
certain environments (the Southeast), influencing a vampire such as
Laurent de Valois, Shane Grimald, or Ramiro first may earn you early
cross-table Sudden Reversals, KRC points, or "i-just-gotta-cycle-cards"
Rushes, along with the sarcastic question "gee, is that a 4-cap with
inferior Dominate?" Frequently, it dies from getting mobbed by 4 other
players. Just as frequently, it gets mobbed and sweeps anyway.

It's not unbeatable, and the current environment has made it somewhat
weaker (lots more +1 intercept, specifically). But it's awfully damn
good.

Nicely done, sir! I think this is my favorite piece on the newsgroup
in some time. I think your reasoning is wrong, mind - but it was
polite, well-written, and thought provoking.

> Nevertheless, it's still hard evidence that Dominate is the strongest
> discipline - better than the ad-hom mudslinging which passes for

> subject line to disassociate myself from it <grin>) Dominate clans

Sure...if there's a 'best' discipline, it might well be Dominate.
Bleeding for a lot is always a good approach if you want to win.
However, I can't agree with your conclusion that victories per
discipline is meaningful when you count it that way. After all,
dominate is a common discipline: if a Ventrue deck wins, you count it
as a victory for presence, dominate, and fortitude; if a Tremere deck
wins, you count it as a victory for thaumaturgy, auspex, and dominate,
and so on. Obviously, the 'rare' disciplines that are found with a
large number of vampires who also have dominate are going to do very
badly under this formula, while the Lasombra, with few Obtenebrators,
will do rather well.

Another way of thinking here is like this: let us suppose that all of
the clans discipline sets - including the Blood Brothers and
Ahrimanes, but not the other Bloodline clans, who haven't won any
tournaments I'm aware of - were equal in strength, and won an equal
amount over 234 games (which is about our sample size). If we compare
the 'expected' victories, based on the presumption that each of the
clan discipline sets is equal in strength, to the actual results, we
can get the deviance - and this works out as:

Disc Vamp Clans Exp V Exp V/V Act V/V Deviance
ani 118 4 52 44 47 +7%
aus 196 6 78 40 42 +6%
cel 156 4 52 33 27 -19%
chi 25 1 13 52 28 -46%
dem 22 1 13 59 41 -31%
dom 172 5 65 38 57 +51%
for 159 5 65 41 35 -14%
nec 41 1 13 32 12 -62%
obf 154 5 65 42 42 -0%
obt 32 1 13 41 53 +30%
pot 167 4 52 31 38 +22%
pre 163 5 65 40 54 +35%
pro 65 2 26 40 28 -30%
qui 28 1 13 46 18 -61%
san* 10 1 4 39 40 +3%
ser 33 1 13 39 24 -39%
spi* 5 1 4 78 40 -49%
thau 71 1 13 18 15 -18%
vic 27 1 13 48 44 -9%

*since these disciplines have only been available for a limited time,
I weighted them at 30% of the victories expected for the others.

'Exp V' means Expected Victories, 'Exp V/V' and 'Act V/V' refer to
victories per vampire with the appropriate discipline.

This suggests that Dominate is indeed overrepresented - followed by
Presence, Obtenebrate, Potence, Animalism, Auspex, Sanguinus, and
Obfuscate, in that order. (My sample size is slightly smaller than
the actual sample; I chose it in order to avoid fractions)

The underrepresented disciplines are, from 'best' to 'worst',
Vicissitude, Fortitude, Thaumaturgy, Celerity, Protean, Dementation,
Serpentis, Chimersty, Spiritus, Quietus, and Necromancy.

I don't think for a moment that this is a very good way of measuring
the strengths of the disciplines, for three reasons.

First, it's my belief that the non-primary clan - primary clan
discipline ratio is higher among the one-clan disciplines like
Thaumaturgy and Protean than it is among the multi-clan disciplines
like Dominate and Potence. I could be wrong - I'm certainly not about
to check.

Second, we're only speculating on the number of vampires in the
winning decks that have the disciplines - it could well be that some
of the winning 'Ventrue' decks had zero fortitude cards and twenty
obfuscate cards, for example. I refuse to try to work out the exact
numbers. =) A great number of basically one-clan decks only play two
of the three disciplines.

Third, and most importantly, we only have access to the winning decks.
In order to have meaningful numbers, we would need to know how many
unsuccessful decks at the tournament level had the relevant
disciplines - I'm going to bet that you'll find that Dominate, for
example, is simply played more at the tournament level than the other
disciplines with a comparable number of vampires - and, if so, it's
hardly surprising that it should win more.

Hannigan

don't think that counting the clans represented by each discipline is
double counting - if the discipline sets were equal in strength, we

enough number of games, no?

Obviously, this ignores the very reasonable argument that the
Brujah/!Brujah, say, just have more vampires to choose from than the
Ahrimanes do, and can just make a better crypt, which will win some
games. But we're just discussing generalities with some numbers
thrown in anyway, right?

would expect the various disciplines to have if they were of equal
strength is useful in determining if some disciplines are overpowered.

the vampires in the winning decks, but trying to infer them from the
listed clans, we should consider also the sum of the disciplines
possessed by all clans that have won tournaments.

count of vampires that considers Assamites and City Gangrel to be
Obfuscate based clans, Toreadors to be a Celerity clan, or Nosferatu

certainly build an Assamite Obfuscate deck, I've wanted to for some
time (basing it on Embraces, Heartblood of the Clan, Khabar:
Community, and even, if you felt inclined, Alamut) - but I've never
actually seen one.

How can I weight something like that? I can't. My own belief is that
Obfuscate is actually a 'better' discipline as Obtenebrate, or that
the two are at least equal; but it would be very hard to prove. I'd
say that maybe 50% of the vampires who have Obfuscate are both
playable and want to have the discipline; I'd say that maybe 75% of

I *am* doing an analysis as I suggested, of the clan-based tournament
winning decks, by percentage of each in-clan (and one condensed
out-of-clan total) discipline based on total discipline-requiring
cards (Sanguine Instruction, etc. excluded), and cards that require
two disciplines count as one of each (thought about doing .5, but

first couple of Brujah decks. Leaning towards operationally defining
a deck as "using" a discipline if it has 15% or more of the
discipline-based cards using that discipline. "Focus" on a discipline
indicates 45% (just a random, nice-sounding number...35% or 40% will
probably be more realistic) of the cards use that discipline.
"Splash" of a discipline indicates some percentage above zero, but
below 15%. If anyone thinks these terms/concepts are useful (or not),
or if the breakpoints should be changed, let me know in this thread.

Significant figures tend to just be 2 digits (meaning 14.8% gets
rounded up to 15%), for obvious reasons. Rounding errors may occur.

One of the winning Assamite decks used Celerity, Quietus, splashed
Obfuscate, and had a heavy proportion (35%) of out-of-clan discipline
cards (auspex and fortitude). The second only used Celerity and
Obfuscate (actually focused on Obfuscate, using my terms) and no
out-of-clans. The third Assamite deck used Obfuscate (44%...almost to
the "focused" breakpoint), and focused on an out-of-clan (presence, at
56%)

Josh's Blood Brothers deck only had clan disciplines in it (is anyone
surprised that Josh built a focused deck?), all of them being "used"

We also find that apparently, Assamite decks only win tournaments in
